subject: Inflated abundance estimates from N-mixture models: a simulation

messages.author: 3a336175c3776dfc
messages.subject: Inflated abundance estimates from N-mixture models: a simulation
parts:
Hi all - thanks for contributing to this group, I have found it very helpful.

I have a question about estimating abundance with N-mixture models via pcount().  I was interested to see how pcount() worked under different probabilities of detection, so I made a dummy simulation (code below). 

I modeled a survey of 20 sites, 3 repeated surveys at each site within year, across 30 years.  For each site, annual abundance was selected from a normal distribution (mean=20, SD=4).  In 4 simulations, I "surveyed" those animals with the desired probability of detection  (for brevity, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, and 0.2 are shown below).  I totaled up the true number of animals across sites within each year (true N) and compared it to the N-hat estimate from pcount().  I also compared the true N to the mean number of animals counted across the 3 replications (raw count) and the maximum number seen at each site across replications (max count).

The results surprised me.  For detection < ~0.6, you get highly inflated estimates of N for 1-10 years out of the 30 simulated.  I believe this is because pcount has estimated p to be low (<0.2) in those years, so N inflates.  This also holds true for sites=50 or mean site abundance=50, but inflation is somewhat less extreme.

My questions:
Is this expected behavior for n-mixture models?  I expected difficulty with very low p, but not with p=0.6 or 0.4.

I estimated N-hat within year - is that an appropriate strategy?

Has anyone else investigated this?

Thank you,
--
Beth Rigby

Doctoral Candidate
Natural Resources Science and Management Program
University of Minnesota



rm(list=ls())
library(unmarked)
set.seed(9)
par(mfrow=c(2,2))
Det<-c(0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2)  ##detection probabilities of interest

for(DD in 1:length(Det)){
 
  NN<-20  ##overall mean abundance across sites
  pp<-Det[DD]  ##detection
  SurveySites<-20
  Years<-30
 
  Data.all.years<-data.frame(TrueN=matrix(nrow=Years, ncol=1))
 
  for(yy in 1:Years){
    data.yy<-data.frame(A=rep(NA,SurveySites),B=rep(NA,SurveySites),C=rep(NA,SurveySites))
    TrueN.i<-rep(NA,SurveySites) 
    for(site.i in 1:SurveySites){
      TrueN.i[site.i]<-round(rnorm(1,NN,4))  ##site-specific abundance
      for(rep.r in 1:3){
        data.yy[site.i,rep.r]<-rbinom(1,TrueN.i[site.i],pp)  ## detection events
      }
    }
   
    NMix.Frame<- unmarkedFramePCount(y=data.yy)
    NMix.null<-  pcount(~1 ~1, NMix.Frame)
   
    Data.all.years[yy,"TrueN"]<-sum(TrueN.i)
   
    Data.all.years[yy,"Null.NSiteEst"]<-coef(backTransform(NMix.null, type="state")) ##N-hat (site)
    Data.all.years[yy,"Null.NAllEst"]<-coef(backTransform(NMix.null, type="state"))*SurveySites ##N-hat (all)
    Data.all.years[yy,"Null.pEst"]<-coef(backTransform(NMix.null, type="det"))   ##p-hat
    Data.all.years[yy,"RawCountAllReps"]<-sum(data.yy)  ##Raw count, all sites&reps, year=yy
    Data.all.years[yy,"MeanRawCountPerRep"]<-sum(data.yy)/3  ##Mean raw count (among reps)
   
    #Maximum count across all 3 replications (index to abundance)
    data.yy$MAX<-NA
    for(ii in 1:nrow(data.yy)){
      data.yy[ii,"MAX"]<-max(data.yy[ii,1:3])
    }
    Data.all.years[yy,"MaxCount"]<-sum(data.yy$MAX) ##Raw Max Count
  }
 
  plot(NULL,NULL, xlab="True N", ylab="Estimator",
       ylim=c(0,max(Data.all.years)), xlim=c(0,max(Data.all.years)),
       main=paste("Mean Site N =",NN, "Detection = ", pp,"\n", SurveySites, "Sites,", Years,"Years"),
       sub="Red=unmarked N-mix, blue=max, black=raw")
  points(Data.all.years$TrueN, Data.all.years$Null.NAllEst, col="red")  ##unmarked estimator vs. truth
  points(Data.all.years$TrueN, Data.all.years$MeanRawCountPerRep)  ## raw count vs. truth (index)
  points(Data.all.years$TrueN, Data.all.years$MaxCount, col="blue")  ##Maximum count across reps vs. truth (index)
  lines(c(0,max(Data.all.years)), c(0,max(Data.all.years)))  ##x=y line
 
}

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Inflated abundance estimates from N-mixture models: a simulation
parts:
hi Beth,
  your results are consistent with what I would expect.
 I think the estimator tends to do worse as expected population sizes increase (or heterogeneity increases), specially with fewer spatial and temporal reps.  In such cases it will help to use a sampling protocol that provides direct information about p (such as double observer or removal or capture-recapture), increase the number of reps, or decrease the size of the spatial units so that E(N) decreases.
 
regards
andy
